claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by replicating selected results from a substantial number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by replicating selected results from a substantial number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
evidence: This is a statement about the purpose and scope of the Reproducibility Project, representing established knowledge about the project's goals.

claim: Delmore and colleagues demonstrated that treatment with JQ1, a small molecular inhibitor targeting BET bromodomains, resulted in the transcriptional down-regulation of the c-Myc oncogene in vitro.
source: Delmore and colleagues demonstrated that treatment with JQ1, a small molecular inhibitor targeting BET bromodomains, resulted in the transcriptional down-regulation of the c-Myc oncogene in vitro (Figure 3B; Delmore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delmore et al., 2011, specifically Figure 3B.

claim: JQ1 treatment significantly reduced disease burden and increased survival time in mice bearing multiple myeloma lesions compared to vehicle-treated control animals.
source: JQ1 treatment significantly reduced disease burden and increased survival time (Figure 7C-E; Delmore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delmore et al., 2011, specifically Figures 7C-E.

claim: c-Myc is a DNA binding transcription factor involved in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis.
source: c-Myc is a DNA binding transcription factor involved in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis (McKeown and Bradner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKeown and Bradner, 2014, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Abnormal expression of c-Myc is frequently observed in a range of malignancies including breast, colon and cervical cancer, small cell lung carcinoma, osteosarcomas, glioblastomas and myeloid leukemias.
source: Abnormal expression of c-Myc is frequently observed in a range of malignancies including breast, colon and cervical cancer, small cell lung carcinoma, osteosarcomas, glioblastomas and myeloid leukemias (Meyer and Penn, 2008; Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meyer and Penn, 2008 and Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014.

claim: c-Myc inactivation leads to tumor regression.
source: While c-Myc expression is required for tumor initiation and maintenance, c-Myc inactivation leads to tumor regression (Felsher and Bishop, 1999; Flores et al., 2004; Soucek et al., 2008; Gabay et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Felsher and Bishop, 1999; Flores et al., 2004; Soucek et al., 2008; Gabay et al., 2014.

claim: c-Myc expression is required for tumor initiation and maintenance.
source: While c-Myc expression is required for tumor initiation and maintenance, c-Myc inactivation leads to tumor regression (Felsher and Bishop, 1999; Flores et al., 2004; Soucek et al., 2008; Gabay et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Felsher and Bishop, 1999; Flores et al., 2004; Soucek et al., 2008; Gabay et al., 2014.

claim: c-Myc represents an enticing target for pharmacological inhibition.
source: Therefore, c-Myc represents an enticing target for pharmacological inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous statements about c-Myc's role in tumor initiation and the effects of its inactivation.

claim: Multiple myeloma is an incurable disease characterized by the unrestricted proliferation of terminally differentiated plasma cells.
source: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable disease characterized by the unrestricted proliferation of terminally differentiated plasma cells (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2011.

claim: The primary tumor-initiating events in multiple myeloma include genetic translocation and hyperploidy.
source: The primary tumor-initiating events include genetic translocation and hyperploidy, while secondary events, such as oncogenic c-Myc activation and overexpression, drive MM progression (Bergsagel and Kuehl, 2005; Morgan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergsagel and Kuehl, 2005 and Morgan et al., 2012.

claim: Secondary events such as oncogenic c-Myc activation and overexpression drive MM progression.
source: The primary tumor-initiating events include genetic translocation and hyperploidy, while secondary events, such as oncogenic c-Myc activation and overexpression, drive MM progression (Bergsagel and Kuehl, 2005; Morgan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergsagel and Kuehl, 2005 and Morgan et al., 2012.

claim: c-Myc activation was prevalent in more than 60% of patient-derived MM cells.
source: Furthermore, studies by Chng and colleagues determined that c-Myc activation was prevalent in more than 60% of patient-derived MM cells (Chng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chng et al., 2011.

claim: Despite therapeutic advances and increases in survival, multiple myeloma patients eventually succumb to treatment-refractory disease.
source: Despite therapeutic advances and increases in survival, patients eventually succumb to treatment-refractory disease (Anderson, 2011; Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2011 and Kumar et al., 2012.

claim: c-Myc lacks a clear ligand-binding domain.
source: Therapeutic strategies targeting c-Myc are complicated by the fact that c-Myc lacks a clear ligand-binding domain (Darnell, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Darnell, 2002.

claim: c-Myc could be disrupted through disruption of chromatin-dependent signaling.
source: However, it is possible that c-Myc could be disrupted by other means, such as through disruption of chromatin-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Bromodomain and extraterminal (BET) proteins are transcriptional regulators that epigenetically control the expression of genes involved in cell cycle, growth and inflammation.
source: Bromodomain and extraterminal (BET) proteins are transcriptional regulators that epigenetically control the expression of genes involved in cell cycle, growth and inflammation (Darnell, 2002; Wu and Chiang, 2007; LeRoy et al., 2008; Dey et al., 2009; Nicodeme et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Darnell, 2002; Wu and Chiang, 2007; LeRoy et al., 2008; Dey et al., 2009; Nicodeme et al., 2010.

claim: BET proteins provide potential therapeutic targets for modulating gene expression programs associated with various human diseases.
source: BETs therefore provide potential therapeutic targets for modulating gene expression programs associated with various human diseases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the role of BET proteins in controlling gene expression.

claim: Bromodomain protein 4 (BRD4) associates with acetylated chromatin to promote transcription.
source: Specifically, bromodomain protein 4 (BRD4), a member of the BET subfamily that associates with acetylated chromatin to promote transcription, was reported to interact with the positive transcription elongation factor complex b (P-TEFb) (Dey et al., 2009; Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dey et al., 2009 and Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: BRD4 was reported to interact with the positive transcription elongation factor complex b (P-TEFb).
source: Specifically, bromodomain protein 4 (BRD4), a member of the BET subfamily that associates with acetylated chromatin to promote transcription, was reported to interact with the positive transcription elongation factor complex b (P-TEFb) (Dey et al., 2009; Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dey et al., 2009 and Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: Recruitment of P-TEFb by c-Myc was reported.
source: Recruitment of P-TEFb by c-Myc was also reported, providing the rationale for Delmore and colleagues to explore targeting BET proteins to inhibit c-Myc transcriptional activity (Bisgrove et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bisgrove et al., 2007.

claim: BRD4 expression was found to positively correlate with MM disease progression.
source: Importantly, BRD4 expression was found to positively correlate with MM disease progression (Delmore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delmore et al., 2011.

claim: JQ1 is a small molecule inhibitor of the BET family of bromodomain-containing proteins.
source: To interrogate this relationship, they used JQ1, a small molecule inhibitor of the BET family of bromodomain-containing proteins, which has the highest affinity with BRD4 and competitively inhibits BET proteins from binding to chromatin (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: JQ1 has the highest affinity with BRD4.
source: To interrogate this relationship, they used JQ1, a small molecule inhibitor of the BET family of bromodomain-containing proteins, which has the highest affinity with BRD4 and competitively inhibits BET proteins from binding to chromatin (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: JQ1 competitively inhibits BET proteins from binding to chromatin.
source: To interrogate this relationship, they used JQ1, a small molecule inhibitor of the BET family of bromodomain-containing proteins, which has the highest affinity with BRD4 and competitively inhibits BET proteins from binding to chromatin (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: The (+)-JQ1 enantiomer potently inhibits BET proteins.
source: While the (+)-JQ1 enantiomer potently inhibits BET proteins, the (−)-JQ1 enantiomer is structurally incapable of inhibiting BET bromodomains supporting an on-target mechanism of action (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: The (−)-JQ1 enantiomer is structurally incapable of inhibiting BET bromodomains.
source: While the (+)-JQ1 enantiomer potently inhibits BET proteins, the (−)-JQ1 enantiomer is structurally incapable of inhibiting BET bromodomains supporting an on-target mechanism of action (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: Gene expression profiling of cells treated with active and inactive forms of JQ1 inhibitor identified MYC as a highly down-regulated gene following BET bromodomain inhibition.
source: Further support for the relationship between c-Myc and BET proteins was reported by Mertz and colleagues, who used gene expression profiling of cells treated with the active and inactive forms of the JQ1 inhibitor to identify MYC as a highly down-regulated gene following BET bromodomain inhibition (Mertz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mertz et al., 2011.

claim: In Figure 3B, Delmore and colleagues assessed the ability of JQ1 to downregulate MYC transcription in the MM cell line MM.1S.
source: In Figure 3B, Delmore and colleagues assessed the ability of JQ1 to downregulate MYC transcription in the MM cell line MM.1S.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach in the cited figure.

claim: JQ1 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in MYC transcripts in MM.1S cells as determined by qRT-PCR.
source: JQ1 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in MYC transcripts as determined by qRT-PCR.
evidence: This claim describes results from Delmore et al., 2011, Figure 3B.

claim: JQ1 was effective at silencing MYC gene transcription.
source: This key experiment shows that JQ1 was effective at silencing MYC gene transcription and will be replicated in Protocol 1.

claim: JQ1 treatment in MM.1S cells significantly decreases MYC mRNA levels.
source: Importantly, Loven and colleagues also recently corroborated these results through the demonstration that JQ1 treatment in MM.1S cells significantly decreases MYC mRNA levels (Loven et al., 2013).

claim: JQ1 potently inhibits MYC in Merkel cell carcinoma cells (MCC-3 and 5) at the transcript level.
source: In addition to MM cell lines, JQ1 has proven to potently inhibit MYC in Merkel cell carcinoma cells (MCC-3 and 5), primary effusion lymphoma cells (PELs) and B cell acute lymphoblastic lymphomas (B-ALL) cells at the transcript level, as well as in diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) cells at the protein expression level (Ott et al., 2012; Shao et al., 2014; Tolani et al., 2014; Trabucco et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Ott et al., 2012; Shao et al., 2014; Tolani et al., 2014; Trabucco et al., 2015.
